Key Information: The following is a short summary of this study to help you decide whether or not to be a part of this study. More detailed information is listed later on in this form.
Why am I being invited to take part in a research study?
We invite you to take part in a research study because you have completed the pre-screening questionnaire and are eligible to participate in this study.
What should I know about a research study?

column2: Whether or not you take part is up to you.
You can choose not to take part.
You can agree to take part and later change your mind.
Your decision will not be held against you.
You can ask all the questions you want before you decide.

column1: Why is this research being done?
The purpose of this study is to investigate people’s motivation to change their personality and become more prosocial.
How long will the research last and what will I need to do?
We expect that you will be in this research study for 30 minutes to complete an online survey.
More detailed information about the study procedures can be found under “What happens if I say yes, I want to be in this research?”
Is there any way being in this study could be bad for me?

Email Communication. This study involves email communication. The security flaws related to this service could expose your identity and involvement in the research to people not associated with the study. While we will work to keep email communications as private as possible, it is not a completely secure form of communication.

There are no significant risks associated with the surveys or behavioral tasks in this study. However, some of the questionnaires contain questions about sensitive topics. You do not have to answer any questions you do not want to answer.
Will being in this study help me in any way?

There are no benefits to you from your taking part in this research. We cannot promise any benefits to others from your taking part in this research. However, possible benefits to others include gaining knowledge about prosociality change motivations.
What happens if I do not want to be in this research?
Participation in research is completely voluntary. You can decide to participate or not to participate.
Your alternative to participating in this research study is to not participate.
Detailed Information: The following is more detailed information about this study in addition to the information listed above.
If you have questions, concerns, or complaints, or think the research has hurt you, talk to the research team at personalityplus@georgetown.edu.

The helpline for the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration is available anytime at 1-800-662-HELP (4357) (for more information, visit https://www.samhsa.gov/find-help/national-helpline). Crisis hotlines and resources (including long-term help) are also available on the American Psychological Association website at https://www.apa.org/topics/crisis-hotlines.
This research has been reviewed and approved by an Institutional Review Board (“IRB”). You may talk to them at (202) 687-1506 or irboard@georgetown.edu if:

column2: Your questions, concerns, or complaints are not being answered by the research team.
You cannot reach the research team.
You want to talk to someone besides the research team.
You have questions about your rights as a research subject.
You want to get information or provide input about this research.

column1: How many people will be studied?
We expect about 500 people will be in this research study.
What happens if I say yes, I want to be in this research?
You will be asked to complete a survey that is expected to take 30 minutes.
What happens if I say yes, but I change my mind later?
You can leave the research at any time. It will not be held against you.
If you decide to leave the research, you will not receive the full compensation for participation.
What happens to the information collected for the research?

Every effort will be made to protect your personal information to the extent allowed by law. Your answers to the questions in this study will not be directly linked to your identity. Records of research study participants are stored and kept indefinitely on a secure cloud storage platform. However, we cannot guarantee absolute confidentiality.

You will not be identified in any reports or publications resulting from this study. In addition to the researchers and research institution(s) conducting this study, organizations that may request to inspect and/or copy your research records for quality assurance data analysis and other research related and operational or administrative purposes, include groups such as: Georgetown University, Georgetown University Institutional Review Board (IRB), federal research oversight agencies.

Researchers are mandated reporters by law. This means that researchers are required by law to report any information about child abuse, elder abuse, and threats to harm yourself or others to the authorities. Everything else you tell us, including any information about past behaviors or substance use, will be protected by the confidentiality protections described above (although not by an NIH Certificate of Confidentiality, which is sometimes applied to studies investigating highly sensitive topics).
Can I be removed from the research without my OK?
The researchers may stop the study or take you out of the study at any time without your approval.

We will compensate you with up to $8 through the online survey platform or Amazon eGift cards. If you enroll in this study through the SONA study pool, you will be compensated with 1 SONA credit for completing the survey and will not be compensated monetarily.

Administrative personnel outside of the research team who are involved in processing your compensation may be aware of your identity (name/email address associated with your Amazon account). They will not have access to your data from the study.

How much does this information make you want to become more prosocial?","When people do prosocial things to help others before or after a stressful event, it can reduce their stress levels. This includes reducing how much stress people feel, as well as body changes associated with stress.

How much does this information make you want to become more prosocial?","In most cultures, doing things to help others is at the core of what it means to be
a good person or a moral person.

How much does this information make you want to become more prosocial?","Helping others is associated with feeling more positive emotions, having better self-esteem, and experiencing fewer symptoms of depression.
How much does this information make you want to become more prosocial?","Helping others is associated with feeling a greater sense of purpose and meaning in life.

How much does this information make you want to become more prosocial?","Helping others can benefit your physical health. People who are more prosocial have lower systemic inflammation, healthier cholesterol levels, and lower body weight.

How much does this information make you want to become more prosocial?","People who are more prosocial tend to be better liked. When people do things to help others, it tends to benefit their reputation.
How much does this information make you want to become more prosocial?","People who are more prosocial tend to feel more connected to other people and have high levels of relationship satisfaction.
How much does this information make you want to become more prosocial?","People who are more prosocial tend to have friends who are more helpful and prosocial as well.
How much does this information make you want to become more prosocial?","People who are more prosocial tend to have better job performance and job satisfaction.

How much does this information make you want to become more prosocial?","People who are more prosocial inspire other people to be more prosocial, too. Thus, helping others creates a prosocial ""ripple effect.""
How much does this information make you want to become more prosocial?","People who are more prosocial are seen as more desirable romantic partners.
